speaker: David Baker
title: Nobel Laureate David Baker on Using AI for Science to Solve Humanity's Biggest Problems
question: In computational biology, how can a traditional experimental lab with no prior machine learning background build frontier AI design models within a few years?
guest: People were surprised that we went from not doing any ML at all to developing cutting-edge ML software from scratch in just a couple years. Mastering the last thirty years of a field is hard, but with ML, where methods move really fast—when we started it was convolutional neural networks, and now they're ancient history and transformers and attention are the thing—it's actually very easy to learn because you don't have to worry about all that ancient history, and the tools are pretty advanced. In my lab, it's one big room: on one side people are sitting at desks doing computer stuff, and on the other side people are pipetting, taking synthetic genes encoding the latest designed proteins, and testing them. As our AI methods got better, we developed rapid ways to make and test proteins from very inexpensive DNA fragments, getting proteins back in about three days. That let us go back and forth between computational methods development and experimental feedback very quickly, which is really the key thing.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A traditional experimental lab can get there by treating its wet-lab capability as the core advantage rather than a handicap. The best-known example is David Baker's lab, which moved from physics-based Rosetta modelling to RoseTTAFold, ProteinMPNN and RFdiffusion in a few years.

The usual recipe has four parts. First, recruit a handful of students or postdocs with machine-learning training and embed them alongside experimentalists, rather than outsourcing to a separate computational group. Second, start from open foundations instead of from scratch: public data such as the Protein Data Bank and sequence databases, and published architectures and open-source code (AlphaFold-style structure predictors, diffusion models, protein language models) that can be fine-tuned or adapted for design. Third, exploit the thing pure-AI groups lack: rapid, high-throughput experimental testing, so every model generation is validated and the results feed back into training as proprietary data. Fourth, secure GPU compute through institutional clusters, cloud credits or industry partnerships.

Deep domain knowledge then guides which problems, representations and benchmarks matter, which is often what separates a useful design model from a merely accurate one.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: A traditional experimental lab’s greatest advantage in AI is its ability to generate proprietary, high-throughput functional data, which remains the primary bottleneck in biological machine learning as model architectures rapidly commoditize. Rather than training models from scratch immediately, the lab should first redesign its wet-lab assays, such as multiplexed screens, to produce standardized datasets capturing quantitative readouts and negative results alongside hits. Simultaneously, it should recruit one or two machine learning postdocs and collaborate with an established AI group, embedding computational researchers directly with bench scientists rather than treating computation as an isolated service. Starting from open-weight biological foundation models and academic or cloud GPU grants, this bilingual team can fine-tune pretrained representations on the lab’s unique experimental data. Running a tight active-learning loop, where models propose designs, experiments rapidly test them, and feedback retrains the model, builds deep institutional fluency alongside an unmatched dataset. Within a few years, this compounding data flywheel and co-evolved expertise enable the lab to scale from fine-tuning existing tools to training its own frontier generative design models.

noweb.answer: A traditional experimental lab can reach the AI frontier not by competing on raw compute or inventing novel architectures, but by turning its wet-lab expertise into a proprietary data engine. In biological design, clean, quantitative experimental data—especially systematic negative results—is far scarcer and more decisive than new algorithms. Rather than pretraining models from scratch, the lab should build atop open-source biological foundation models and cloud compute, embedding one or two experienced machine learning leads directly alongside bench scientists or forming a deep partnership with a computational group. Together, they must redesign experiments around model training from day one: scaling throughput with multiplexed assays or automation, enforcing strict metadata and reproducibility standards, and sampling diverse, informative regions of sequence or chemical space rather than only chasing single hits. This foundation enables a tight active-learning loop where fine-tuned generative and predictive models propose designs, wet-lab assays rapidly test them, and every outcome updates the model. Within two to three years, compounding task-specific datasets and fast design-build-test-learn cycles yield specialized design models that outperform generalist frontier systems on the lab’s target biology.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The common recipe is to use your experimental strengths and bring in the ML expertise you lack. Patrick Hsu's lab at the Arc Institute is a good example. It started as a CRISPR and genome-engineering lab. By partnering with ML researchers such as Brian Hie and hiring computational talent, it produced the Evo genome language models in roughly two to three years. In 2025 the group reported using Evo to design working bacteriophage genomes.

The strategies that make this possible are a few. First, recruit or co-lead with people who already know modern deep learning, and don't try to retrain biologists from scratch. Second, build on open architectures, public sequence databases and existing tools like AlphaFold, ESM and RFdiffusion, and get compute through partnerships with industry or national labs. Third, put the most effort into what an experimental lab does best. That means generating large, high-quality, purpose-built datasets and running tight design-build-test-learn loops, so wet-lab validation feeds back into model training. Finally, pick biological problems where the lab's experimental know-how gives it an edge.

My searches didn't find a source discussing this exact question, so the Arc example is my own pick for illustrating the approach.

noweb.answer: A wet lab's main advantage is something most ML groups lack: the ability to generate proprietary, high-quality experimental data and test designs quickly. The successful path usually builds on that. First, the lab hires or partners with a few strong computational people, often ML-trained students or postdocs drawn by access to real biology, and gives them real ownership rather than treating them as service staff. Second, it starts from open-source foundation models such as protein language models, AlphaFold-style structure predictors, and diffusion design tools, then fine-tunes them rather than training from scratch. Third, it redesigns its experiments for machine learning, using high-throughput assays, deep mutational scanning, and standardized, well-annotated datasets that include negative results, so each experimental round produces training data. Fourth, it runs tight design–build–test–learn loops, letting models propose candidates and feeding the measurements back for retraining. Finally, it secures compute through cloud credits, institutional clusters, or industry collaborations, and benchmarks openly against established groups. Within a few years, this combination of unique data, fast validation, and borrowed architectures can produce frontier-level design models.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Start with a design problem the lab can measure reliably, such as improving an industrial enzyme’s stability. Hire an experienced ML lead and pair them with experimentalists who understand the assay. In the first year, use existing pretrained models as baselines and build a reproducible dataset that records assay conditions, failed designs, and batch effects.

Then run repeated design–build–test–learn cycles. Use the model to propose candidates, test them in the lab, and feed the results back into training. Compare each iteration with simple baselines on held-out families and in prospective experiments. Scale up data collection and training where those results show clear gains.

Within a few years, a lab can plausibly reach the frontier on a well-defined design task. Its advantage is the ability to generate reliable measurements that public datasets lack and use them to steer the model.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A traditional lab can reach the frontier within a few years by choosing a narrow design problem where it can test candidates quickly and reliably. Its strongest starting asset is often an assay that measures the property it wants to improve. For example, a lab developing a fluorescent sensor can measure how strongly the sensor responds to its target.

Early on, recruit a computational scientist or partner with an ML group. Start with a pretrained model and compare its designs with candidates chosen by the lab’s usual method. Test both under the same conditions and keep the failures as well as the successes. Use those measurements to adapt the model, then repeat the cycle with fresh candidates.

Judge progress by how often new designs meet a prespecified experimental target and how much testing each success takes. A credible frontier result is a reproducible advantage over the best available methods on that task.
